newsitem.title: USA: MCI-BT deal would likely win US govt ok - experts.
newsitem.headline: MCI-BT deal would likely win US govt ok - experts.

text.p: A combination of MCI Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc probably would pass U.S. regulatory muster, given that the U.K. telecommunications market is one of the most open in the world, lawyers and analysts said Friday.
"It appears this deal would pass (Federal Communications Commission) approval at first glance," said analyst Scott Cleland of the Washington Research Group of Schawb Capital Markets.

Experts noted that an FCC rule adopted last year permits a foreign carrier to invest in a U.S. carrier in excess of a 25 percent cap -- as long as the overseas company's home market is open for competition from U.S. telecommunications companies.
Under the rule, adopted last November, an investment stake of more than 25 percent by a foreign phone company triggers an automatic FCC review of that company's home market.

Scott Harris, a former head of the FCC's international bureau and now an attorney with Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher, said that other than the U.S. telecommunications market, the British market is the "most open" in the world.
Harris said the biggest hurdle such a transaction would face is the market power it would have on certain phone routes, especially between the U.S. and U.K.

He noted that because of competitive concerns, curbs already were put in place after BT's acquisition of its initial 20 percent stake in MCI. Harris suggested those kinds of competitive concerns would probably be revisited if an MCI-BT merger were indeed struck.
In 1994, the U.S. Justice Department reached a consent agreement with BT and MCI that prevents discrimination against U.S. carriers that offer multinational services.
The agreement also contains safeguards ensuring non-discriminatory access in the future.
Among other things, the MCI-BT venture was required to publish rates and other information. And it was barred from gaining secret pricing data about U.S. competitors.
And while certain conditions could be imposed on an outright MCI-BT merger, any deal still is expected to pass.
"The FCC probably would conclude that the British market is open," said attorney Alfred Mamlet of Steptoe & Johnson.
The FCC, as is customary in such a situation, declined to comment.
The agency, in general, must determine whether such transactions are in the "public interest." Its main focus, however, is the openness of the foreign company's own market, lawyers said.
The agency also can look at the impact of a deal on competition in the United States. And it can look at trade considerations.
